ours.name: West Ridge
ours.approach: Start at the Esmeralda Trailhead (end of North Fork Teanaway Road, ~4,243 ft) and follow the Ingalls Way Trail. At about 0.3 mile, stay right onto Ingalls Way where it leaves the Esmeralda Basin Trail; at about 1.7 miles (5,440 ft), turn right at the Longs Pass junction rather than continuing to Ingalls Basin, and switchback up open slopes to Longs Pass (roughly 3 mi, ~2,100 ft gain from the trailhead, cresting around 6,400 ft) — the pass gives the first clear look at Stuart's west aspect. From the pass, descend steep, sometimes dusty/scree-y trail on the north side, losing about 1,300 ft in a mile, to reach Ingalls Creek in the timber below. ours.descent: Descend via the Cascadian Couloir, the standard walk-off for the entire Stuart massif — this is a scramble descent, not a rappel route, under normal (dry to firm-snow) conditions. From the summit, reverse the short 3rd/2nd-class scramble east along the summit ridge to the false summit (~9,200 ft), then drop into the broken rock and scree above the top of the couloir. fktText: Description "Without a rival as the crown peak in the central Cascades of Washington, Mount Stuart has been pronounced the single greatest mass of exposed granite in the United States...its northern and eastern faces are the alpine climax of the Wenatchee Mountains. They make a powerful impact on first sight...The mountaineering problems are magnified by the mountain's massive dimensions and its complexity." - excerpted from Fred Beckey's "Cascade Alpine Guide" Overlooking the Kittitas Valley and visible from many other nearby mountains, Mt. Stuart is an icon of Central Washington. Sitting at 9,415ft, this beautiful mountain attracts many climbers during the summer months. The primary FKT route starts at the Ingalls Lake trailhead, goes up and over Longs Pass to Ingalls Creek, and ascends the Cascadian Couloir to the summit. Descent is by the same route. https://www.mountaineers.org/activities/routes-places/ingalls-stuart-area-review/mt-stuart-cascadian-couloir The West Ridge is the second most commonly climbed route on the mountain. It includes low fifth class climbing, a great deal of scrambling, and significant route-finding challenges. ours.name: Standard Scramble (above Lake Cushman)
ours.approach: From the T-intersection at the end of North Lake Cushman Road, continue right onto FS Road 24 for about 1.5 miles, then turn left onto FS Road 2419 and follow it up the Big Creek drainage for roughly 6.6 miles to its end at a small trailhead/parking area at about 3,026 ft. From here the 'trail' quickly becomes a boot path and then largely off-trail scrambling — there is no numbered maintained trail for most of the route. fktText: Description Start at the Mt Washington trailhead, which is nearby the mt ellinor trailheads. it starts off super steep and stays that way the entire time. It starts forested, then there is a scree field crossing. After that, there is another short forested section before coming into a meadow. Then, you continue on another scree field, before starting the scrambling section. You walk up a switchback, and then walk along the ridge for a little while. When almost at the summit, stay right and go around the right side of a boulder, and then the summit is right there. ours.name: South Slopes
ours.approach: Start at the Stafford Creek Trailhead (Trail #1359), Cle Elum Ranger District, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, at the end of Stafford Creek Road (FR 9703), which leaves North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737) past 29 Pines Campground — a small, often-overflowing lot for roughly 20 cars (Northwest Forest Pass required). From the trailhead, Stafford Creek Trail #1359 climbs at a gentle-to-moderate grade through dry ponderosa/lodgepole forest, staying close to Stafford Creek for the first mile (a short rerouted, steeper switchback section around 0.5 mile bypasses old avalanche-damaged tread). The trail continues gaining gradually along the creek — figure roughly 3,000 ft of gain spread ove
ours.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: drop off the summit back down the broad south/southeast ridge to Navaho Pass (easy Class 2 scrambling, no rope or rappelling needed), then rejoin Stafford Creek Trail #1359 and retrace it past the Moon Landing section, the meadow camp/water source, the Standup Creek Trail (#1369) junction at ~3.5–3.8 miles, and back down along Stafford Creek to the trailhead.

fktText: Description This is a relatively popular, out and back single-track route to tag Navaho Peak in the Teanaway region. The route has a stunning view of the Stewart range/backside of the very popular Enchantments in Washington. The route starts at the Stafford Creek Trailhead and travels up the Stafford Creek Trail until it intersects the Old County Line Trail. Turn right on the Old County Line Trail and then left at the fork to head up Navaho Peak. Tag the peak and travel back down the same route. ours.name: Painted Traverse
ours.approach: From the North Fork Sauk trailhead, the Red Mountain (Painted Mountain Lookout) Trail branches left about 100 yards in and climbs about a mile to the old lookout site near 3,100 ft. Beyond it an unmaintained climber's path goes straight up the slope with almost no switchbacks, including a short cliff band that needs class 3 scrambling, and continues steeply to the summit of Painted Mountain. Expect close to 5,000 ft of gain in under three miles.
ours.descent: From White Mountain descend its south ridge to White Pass on the Pacific Crest Trail, then follow the North Fork Sauk Trail down switchbacks and through old-growth forest back to the trailhead. Parties that stop at Portal Peak can instead drop to Red Pass and take the same trail down.

ours.name: Ragged Ridge
ours.approach: From the Easy Pass Trailhead on SR-20, hike the Easy Pass Trail about 3.5 miles and roughly 2,900 ft to Easy Pass, about 6,500 ft. Most parties then leave the trail and sidehill west along the south side of the ridge on grassy benches around 6,600-6,800 ft, crossing many small gullies and buttresses; a large gully with a waterfall just before the basin needs a short descent of steep scree. The usual high camp is in the basin just south of Mesahchie Peak at about 6,600-6,700 ft, roughly five hours from the car. The alternative is to follow the trail down the far side of the pass into the Fisher Creek basin near 5,100 ft and climb off-trail back up to the same camp. From camp, climb northwest
ours.descent: Trip reports consistently recommend dropping off the ridge to the Fisher Creek trail (roughly 2-2.5 hrs from the Cosho/west end) rather than attempting a high traverse back at 7,000+ ft, which is described as slow, exposed sidehilling through 'awfulness'; from Fisher Creek, follow the maintained trail back over Easy Pass to the trailhead.

fktText: Description "Ragged Ridge" is a coveted link-up in the Washington mountaineering community. Many "light and fast" enthusiasts test their mettle to see if they can complete the entire ridge of 4 peaks within daylight hours. Not all succeed. Just finishing car-to-car in a day is a feather in the cap of any mountain athlete. On loose, steep terrain these 21 miles, with mixed 3rd and 4th class climbing to gain summits, are a real test piece. These are not for the casual runner. This is not forgiving terrain. Experience with exposure, loose rock, scrambling and route finding are an absolute pre-requisite for an attempt on this ridge. Starting and finishing at Easy Pass Trailhead , there are 4 required high points on the traverse - Mesachie (8795') , Katsuk (8680') , Kimtah (8600') , and Cosho (8332') - they may be tagged in any order, so long as all are tagged before returning to the car. (GPS + photos on true summits for substantiation) After all four peaks are tagged, there are the options of returning on the high traverse of ledges/steep terrain or dropping to the easy pass trail below, both of which involve steep technical terrain. In his blog, Sean O'Rourke lays claim to having completed this link up in 14hrs car-to-car and he certainly has the resume to back up that kind of claim on this type of terrain . In my opinion, it should be considered the time to beat for Ragged Ridge As far as times with GPS substantiation for us young-guns where GPS'ing everything is the norm, Jas

ours.name: Southeast Ridge
ours.approach: From Winthrop, drive Highway 20 west about 14-15 miles to the Mazama junction, then turn onto Lost River Road (County Road 9140) and drive about 7.5 paved miles and another 1.5 miles on gravel Forest Road 5400 to Robinson Creek Trailhead (elev. ~2,500-2,560 ft, with an information sign, picnic table, and vault toilet). From the trailhead, hike the Robinson Creek - Middle Fork Trail (#478) north for about 2.8 miles to the signed/bridged Beauty Creek junction (elev. ~3,560 ft) just past a bridge over Beauty Creek. Turn right (northeast/uphill) onto the unmarked, overgrown Beauty Creek Trail and follow it about 1.5 miles up the valley, staying northwest of the creek, to a tributary crossing aro
ours.descent: From the summit, reverse the ridge scramble south-east along the crest back to the gap, downclimb the scree slope to the tarn basin, then follow the boot path/open slopes back down to the Beauty Creek tributary crossing (~5,200 ft) and down the steep, brushy Beauty Creek Trail to its junction with the Robinson Creek Trail. fktText: Description Robinson Mountain (8,731') is located in western Okanogan County in Washington state. It is part of the Okanogan Range which is a sub-range of the North Cascades . The mountain is situated in the Pasayten Wilderness , on land administered by Okanogan National Forest . It is an idyllic climb, reminding some of the Swiss Alps. Its combination of trail, snow travel, and class 3 scrambling lends a very enjoyable context for moving fast, car-to-car. Read more on local geology here . Read more about the route here or here . ours.name: SE Ridge AKA Shield Wall
ours.approach: From the road-end parking on Forest Road 2419 (off North Lake Cushman Road/FR-24), shared with the standard route, walk the old roadbed past the standard route's trail entrance to just beyond the Big Creek crossing (~3,100 ft); a way trail leads to the base of the southeast ridge's rock section. Follow an old roadbed across Big Creek and a climbers' trail up a rock rib, gaining roughly 1,600 ft to a bowl below the Shield Wall; a gully ascends up and left to a notch at the wall's left corner (~4,850 ft) where the technical climbing begins.
ours.descent: The route finishes on the summit ridge of Mount Washington, and the way down is the standard route rather than the SE Ridge, which would mean many rappels and the fifth-class cracks in reverse. Descend the Class 3-4 scramble to the basin; lingering snow often covers the upper slopes in early summer, and the narrow hourglass constriction can be bypassed on its west side. ours.name: South Headwall
ours.approach: Northeast via Ingalls Way Trail #1390 and Longs Pass Trail #1229, then down to Ingalls Creek; ascend first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir
ours.descent: The route tops out very close to the true summit, so the way down is the Cascadian Couloir to the south. Cross the Class 2-3 ground between the true and false summits (steep, often corniced snow early in the season), then drop into the couloir and follow it down loose scree and talus to Ingalls Creek. ours.name: Southeast Ridge (SE Corner)
ours.approach: East-northeast up Shannon Ridge, then traverse Sulphide Glacier to reach southeast ridge base
ours.descent: Rappel the same 4th-class gully used as the standard ascent line up the summit pyramid (the line shared with the Fisher Chimneys/Sulphide Glacier finish); a 60m rope reaches all belay stations.

fktText: Description https://www.mountaineers.org/explore/routes-places/mt-shuksan-sulphide-glacier A 7 mile forest approach to a gentle glacier climb in the North Cascades that ends with a 500 feet snow (early season) or rock scramble up the summit pyramid. Impressive views of Mount Baker and the North Cascade peaks. If the summit rock is icy, evaluate carefully and perhaps forgo summit. Times: 5-6 hr hike to camp, and 5-6 hr from camp to summit. ours.name: Upper North Ridge w/Great Gendarme
ours.approach: From I-90 Exit 85, take Highway 970 east 7 miles to Teanaway Road, then bear right onto North Fork Teanaway Road continuing 22.5 miles total. From trailhead: via Lake Ingalls and Stuart Pass to Goat Pass, then east across the Stuart Glacier to the North Ridge notch
ours.descent: From the true summit, travel southeast on blocky 3rd/4th-class terrain toward the false summit, follow cairns down into the Cascadian Couloir snowfield, then descend extended 3rd-class scree/talus to Ingalls Creek. Sherpa Glacier or a Sherpa Pass glissade are faster early-season alternatives for parties returning to a north-side camp.
